title: The placental membrane: thin, not a wall

objective.text: Explain what the placental membrane separates and what passes across it.

body.general: Is the placenta a wall that keeps everything out? No; it is a thin membrane, not a true barrier [f6]. It keeps the mother's and the baby's blood apart [f1]. Early on it has four cell layers [f3]. From month 4 many places thin to two: the syncytium (the merged outer layer of the villus) and the baby's capillary lining [f4]. Oxygen, food and salts pass easily [f6,f7]. So do the mother's antibodies of the IgG type, which protect the baby [f8]. Most drugs and many viruses cross too [f10].
body.mbbs: The placental membrane separates maternal and fetal blood, which normally do not mix [f1]. A few fetal cells still escape through small breaks in it [f2]. Initially it has four layers: fetal endothelium, villous connective tissue, cytotrophoblast and syncytium [f3]. From month 4 many villi lose cytotrophoblast and core tissue, leaving syncytium and endothelium [f4]. Because maternal blood directly bathes chorion-derived syncytium, the placenta is haemochorial [f5]. It is not a true barrier [f6]. Gases cross by simple diffusion, so fetal oxygen supply depends on placental blood flow [f6]. Nutrients and electrolytes pass readily [f7]. Maternal IgG crosses from about week 14 after fertilization, giving passive immunity [f8]. Steroid hormones cross easily; thyroxine crosses slowly [f11]. Most drugs and many viruses, such as rubella, cytomegalovirus, varicella and measles, cross too [f10].

facts.text: The placental membrane separates maternal from fetal blood; normally the two do not mix.
A few fetal blood cells still leak into the mother's blood through tiny breaks in the membrane.
At first the membrane has four layers: the lining of fetal capillaries (endothelium), villus connective tissue, cytotrophoblast and syncytium.
From month 4 many villi lose their cytotrophoblast and much core tissue, leaving syncytium and endothelium, which speeds exchange.
Maternal blood directly bathes a layer made by the chorion, so the human placenta is called haemochorial.
The membrane is not a true barrier: oxygen and carbon dioxide cross by simple diffusion, so supply depends mainly on blood flow.
Nutrients and electrolytes cross the membrane readily.
The mother's IgG antibodies cross from about week 14 after fertilization, giving the fetus passive immunity.
facts.note: R05bb: fetal IgG rises from early in the second trimester

facts.text: A child reaches adult IgG levels only by about age 3.
Most drugs and many viruses cross, including rubella, cytomegalovirus, varicella and measles.
Steroid hormones cross easily; thyroxine crosses only slowly.
If the mother uses heroin or cocaine, the fetus can become dependent on the drug.
Fetal red cells that leak across can lead the mother to make antibodies against them, as in Rh disease.
At term the fetus takes up about 20–30 mL of oxygen a minute.
Synthetic progestins given in pregnancy can masculinize female fetuses, and the drug DES caused vaginal cancer and reproductive-tract defects.
Beyond Langman: IgG is the only antibody class that crosses; the FcRn receptor on the syncytiotrophoblast carries it across.

misconceptions.wrong: The placenta is a barrier that protects the baby from drugs and germs.
misconceptions.right: Most drugs and many viruses cross the placental membrane freely.

misconceptions.wrong: Maternal and fetal blood mix in the placenta.
misconceptions.right: A membrane keeps them apart, though a few fetal red cells leak across.

misconceptions.wrong: Maternal antibodies of every class protect the fetus.

checks.prompt: A pregnant woman asks whether the placenta will keep a medicine away from her baby. Which answer is right?
options: No: most drugs cross the placental membrane
Yes: the placenta blocks all drugs
checks.why: The placental membrane is not a true barrier; most drugs and many viruses cross it.

checks.prompt: Which class of maternal antibody crosses to the fetus?
checks.why: Only IgG crosses, from about week 14, lending the baby the mother's protection.

checks.prompt: From month 4, which layers separate the two bloods in many places?
options: Syncytium and the fetal capillary lining
Fetal capillary lining and villus connective tissue
checks.why: In many places the inner cell layer and core tissue are lost, leaving only syncytium over the fetal capillary lining.

adult: After birth the baby is still protected by the mother's IgG; its own levels reach adult values only by about age 3 [f8,f9].
clinical: Most drugs and many viruses, such as rubella and cytomegalovirus, can reach the fetus [f10]. If a mother uses heroin or cocaine, her baby can be born dependent on the drug [f12]. Because a few fetal red cells leak across, a mother can make antibodies against her baby's red cells, as in Rh disease [f2,f13].

remember.q: Do maternal and fetal blood mix in the placenta?
remember.a: No; the placental membrane keeps them apart, though a few fetal cells leak across [f1,f2].

remember.q: Which maternal antibody crosses the placenta?
remember.a: IgG, from about week 14 after fertilization: protection borrowed from the mother [f8].

remember.q: Which layers remain in many places after month 4?
remember.a: Syncytium and the fetal capillary lining [f4].
